draft.title: Autobiographical memory and imagining the future
card: Autobiographical memory is memory of your own life. It draws on episodic memory (specific events, with when and where) and semantic memory (facts, such as the name of your school).

Imagining a future event also uses both systems. Episodic memory supplies details from past events to build a new scene. Semantic memory supplies facts and knowledge about the people and places involved.

Because recalling the past and imagining the future share these systems, damage to them often affects both. A person who cannot recall past events in detail may also struggle to imagine detailed future ones.
This is a link, not a rule. Imagining the future is not simply recalling the past, but it relies on the same stored material.
draft.remember: The same memory systems help us recall our past and imagine our future, so losing one often weakens the other.

a.q: Why might a person with damaged episodic memory also find it hard to imagine a future holiday in detail?
opts: Both tasks draw on episodic memory for details
Imagining the future relies only on semantic memory
Future events are stored as past events in memory
Episodic memory only stores plans for the future
a.why: Imagining a future event builds a new scene from details of past events, which come from episodic memory. Semantic memory helps too, so it is not the only system used, and damage to episodic memory can weaken both tasks.
a.clue: Where do the details for a new imagined scene come from?

b.q: After a brain injury, Liam can name every street in his town but cannot recall his last birthday party or picture his next one in detail. What best explains this?
opts: Episodic memory is affected, which both tasks rely on
Semantic memory is affected, which both tasks rely on
Past and future events are stored in different systems
Imagining the future never uses memory of past events
b.why: Liam still has facts about streets, so semantic memory is working. He struggles with recalling and imagining specific events, which both depend on episodic memory. Blaming semantic memory is tempting, but his facts are intact.
b.clue: Which of his abilities still works, and which has been lost?

a.best: Both tasks draw on episodic memory for details

b.best: Episodic memory is affected, which both tasks rely on

problems.detail: 'Losing one often weakens the other' is ambiguous. Just before it, 'the same memory systems' (episodic and semantic) is the nearest plural noun, so a student may read it as losing one memory system weakens the other system. The card actually says damage to the shared systems affects both recalling the past and imagining the future. It should say 'losing the ability to recall the past in detail often weakens imagining the future'.

check.summary: The card and both questions are accurate and fit the VCE study design. The remember line's 'losing one often weakens the other' could be misread as one memory system weakening the other, and should name recall and imagining explicitly.
